In [[computational geometry]], the positive and negative '''Voronoi poles''' of a [[cell (geometry)|cell]] in a [[Voronoi diagram]] are certain vertices of the diagram, chosen in pairs in each cell of the diagram to be far from the site generating that pair. They have applications in [[surface reconstruction]].

==Definition==
[[File:Voronoi diagram with poles.svg|480px|center|'''Example''' <br>Here {{mvar|x}} is the positive pole of {{mvar|V{{sub|p}}}} and {{mvar|y}} its negative. As the cell corresponding to {{mvar|q}} is unbounded, only the negative pole {{mvar|z}} exists.]]

Let <math>V</math> be the Voronoi diagram for a set of sites <math>P</math>, and let <math>V_p</math> be the Voronoi cell of <math>V</math> corresponding to a site <math>p\in P</math>. If <math>V_p</math> is bounded, then its '''positive pole''' is the vertex of the boundary of <math>V_p</math> that has maximal distance to the point <math>p</math>. If the cell is unbounded, then a positive pole is not defined.{{r|jdb}}

Furthermore, let <math>\bar{u}</math> be the vector from <math>p</math> to the positive pole, or, if the cell is unbounded, let <math>\bar{u}</math> be a vector in the average direction of all unbounded Voronoi edges of the cell. The '''negative pole''' is then the Voronoi vertex <math>v</math> in <math>V_p</math> with the largest distance to <math>p</math> such that the vector <math>\bar{u}</math> and the vector from <math>p</math> to <math>v</math> make an angle larger than <math>\tfrac{\pi}{2}</math>.{{r|jdb}}

== History and application==
The poles were introduced in 1998 in two papers by [[Nina Amenta]], Marshall Bern, and [[Manolis Kellis]], for the problem of [[surface reconstruction]]. As they showed, any [[smooth surface]] that is sampled with sampling density inversely proportional to its [[curvature]] can be accurately reconstructed, by constructing the [[Delaunay triangulation]] of the combined set of sample points and their poles, and then removing certain triangles that are nearly parallel to the line segments between pairs of nearby poles.{{r|ab|abk}}
